An environment is a complete, separately governed copy of your model — sources, tables, policies, masking rules and grants. Teams keep a dev environment to change the model in, a staging one to review it in, and prod to serve from, then move the change forward by merging one environment into the next with a diff, an approval and an undoable history.

Your sandbox IS one of these environments, minted for you alone. Managing them — creating, merging, deploying, retiring — belongs to the organization that owns them, so the surface is shown here rather than handed over: you can see what it does, and it acts on nothing.

he/securityPage.json::securityPage.purpo: Scope a rule to a single table, or to a whole domain so it covers every table in it; where both apply, the table rule wins for that table. A rule on a tag covers every table carrying the tag, now and later, and is added to the table's own rule: a tag can only narrow what a role reads. A rule is written against a role rather than a person, so what someone can see is changed by changing the role they hold.

A row-level security rule is a SQL predicate bound to one role and one scope. The server ANDs it into the query before execution — on reads and on writes, whichever surface the request arrives on — so a role sees only the rows its rule permits and cannot opt out by picking a different client.
he/securityPage.json::securityPage.roleP: A role also carries its own ceilings: requests per second, and limits on query depth, node count, and execution time. That is how a role can be given reach without being given unbounded cost — an expensive query is refused by the role that issued it, not by the source it would have hit.

A role is the unit every other permission is written against. Its capabilities decide which operations it may run, and its domain access decides which parts of the model it can reach at all. Row-level rules, and the access checks on every surface, name a role rather than a person — so what someone can see and do is changed by changing the role they hold.

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. It decides whether the materialized view is ONE copy shared by all instances, or a separate copy per instance. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot — pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy independently — simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so only safe for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Where the copy lives depends on the federation engine's store: per-instance only makes sense when each instance has its OWN store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a SHARED external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared — per-instance has nowhere private to write and would just clobber.

he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.des: Human-readable description shown in the API schema (SDL), data catalog, and AI-assisted query generation. Good descriptions improve auto-generated SQL accuracy.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.dra: Out of service while checked: read and written nowhere, offered in no schema, and copied nowhere — existing copies in every region are removed. A table or view registered here starts as draft; clear it to release it.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.exp: The preflight gate: the period is closed only once its inputs are fresh-through the window boundary. Default = every SQL-lineage input. Uncheck to name a custom set (or none = calendar-only, verify nothing).
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.fre: Source-native query returning one comparable token; blank → MAX(watermark). Provisa compares stored vs. fresh by equality and re-pulls only on change.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.gra: When a version is cut: a nesting period (daily…annual), or a custom Outlook/iCalendar recurrence.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.hid: You can change how this table's columns are hidden: who sees each column, its masks, and the fakes and synthetic rules of its sensitive columns. Registering, renaming and the table's other settings need the Table registration right.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.inc: Apply the input's reported changes to the prior landed state instead of re-running the query — the classic way to keep a derived table cheaply in sync with a source's change stream (CDC), applying its inserts/updates by key each refresh rather than recopying the whole source. It maintains CURRENT state (no versions). The same change stream commonly feeds a SEPARATE history table too: this incremental table is the live mirror, while a Time Travel delta MV off the same deltas appends each change as a new version — one stream, two tables (current + full history). Requires a primary key and an incrementalizable view; an infeasible declaration is rejected at registration.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.loa: Fix the Load Management and Timeliness settings before saving.
How current the data must be for each reader, balanced against load on the platform and upstream sources.

Balances how current each reader's data is against load on the platform and on upstream sources. Ideally the upstream manages its own load; the operator protects the platform, and the upstream when it can't protect itself. These settings are the operator's floor — no query or request hint can get fresher data or put more load on a source than they allow. Readers can only choose to accept older data for speed. A table the engine reads live ignores the TTL settings; they apply once it is served from its replica (Replicate, or Load Protected).
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.loc: This deployment uses an embedded federation engine and materializes into an instance-local store. If you are running more than one instance, each instance keeps its own copy of this view and they may briefly differ until they converge (eventual consistency). To have every instance read one shared copy, set a shared materialization store (a central Store URL in Settings) or use a different federation engine. A single instance is unaffected.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.mat: Precompute THIS view's SQL into a stored cache table (CTAS into mv_cache) on the Refresh Interval below. Distinct from 'Replicate' above, which keeps a copy of a raw source table in the store — this materializes a Provisa-defined view.

Comma-separated column(s) identifying a row — required for upsert persistence and for incremental maintenance.

he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.nam: Controls how the alias is cased in the API schema. snake_case → my_table, camelCase → myTable, PascalCase → MyTable. 'Inherit' uses the source's convention. Affects GraphQL field names, Cypher labels, and SDL output.

he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.nrt: NRT debounce: a burst of upstream changes collapses into one recompute. Quiet = seconds of calm before firing (0 = real-time). Max delay = the hard staleness cap under continuous churn.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.off: Inherited: this table's source is read only on schedule.
IANA timezone the off-peak window is evaluated in (e.g. UTC, America/New_York). Tracks DST.

he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.per: How each update is written to the MV's store. Its options depend on Time Travel (keep history): OFF stores current state only — replace (overwrite everything) or upsert (merge by primary key); ON keeps history — snapshot (append the whole fresh result as a new version each refresh) or delta (append only the rows that changed, plus tombstones for deletes). Snapshot/delta are the bitemporal storage modes, which the engine uses in place of replace/upsert.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.pre: Optional preflight check run after the view SQL and before landing: define preflight(streams, ctx) and return a VERDICT — ctx.ok() to continue, ctx.abort(reason) to reject (error + poison downstream), or ctx.quarantine(reason) to hold without landing. streams is a dict keyed by input node: streams["schema.table"] yields that input's rows lazily, so you inspect an input without materializing it. A check inspects; it does NOT transform rows (put transforms in SQL or an external processor). A SQL-expressible check — if any(...)/all(...) over one input's rows — is pushed down to the engine as a count probe over that input, so it scales to a billion rows; anything else streams each input as Arrow batches and short-circuits. Call ctx.warn(reason) for a non-fatal advisory. It MUST be deterministic — no clock, randomness, imports, or IO — and is purity-checked when you save; a non-deterministic or unsafe check is rejected.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.pro: How the freshness probe detects change, gated by source type. watermark → append (fetch rows past MAX(watermark)); hash → replace (content token, e.g. ETag/checksum); count → replace (row-count delta, coarse); none → replace on cadence (the output content-hash still suppresses an unchanged ripple). Auto = resolve per source class.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.ref: How often the materialized view is rebuilt (CTAS into mv_cache). Governs freshness of the stored table that QUERIES read. Distinct from Cache TTL (which caches query results) and from Poll interval (which paces the live change stream to subscribers).

Fix the Role TTL rows before saving.

Per-role staleness tolerance for this table, in seconds. A role's effective TTL is the larger of the Cache TTL and its entry here, so an entry can only let that role accept older data; it never makes data fresher than the Cache TTL allows.
Enter a whole number of seconds, 0 or more.
Roles not listed use the Cache TTL ({{sec}}s).
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.sco: domain: served to roles that reach this table's domain. public: also to roles outside it. restricted: only to the roles named in Visible to.
he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.sql: The GraphQL/Cypher field name exposed in the API. Defaults to the table name. Changing this renames the entity across all queries and SDL docs.

he/tableEditForm.json::tableEditForm.upd: Keeps history (time travel), compactly. Every refresh appends ONLY the rows that changed (plus tombstones for deletes) as new versions — you can still query 'as of' any time, but storage grows only by the change, not the whole result. The classic way to maintain a full change history / audit trail of a source without storing a full copy each refresh. Needs an entity key to identify the entity across versions.

The query is NOT re-run. The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key — so work per refresh scales with the SIZE OF THE CHANGE, not the whole dataset. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It applies only when all three hold: (1) exactly ONE input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta — i.e. it runs on a change/CDC signal, not full snapshots, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column) so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. Also needs a primary key. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), it falls back to a full recompute for that refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct. Work per refresh scales with the TOTAL size of the inputs, not with how much actually changed.

Keeps history (time travel). Every refresh appends the ENTIRE fresh result as a new version stamped with its time — you can query the table 'as of' any past refresh. Simplest history model and works on any engine, but storage grows by the full result size every refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key: matching rows are updated in place, new rows inserted, nothing deleted-and-reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size — only the write is by key.

he/tour.json::tour.demos.files.title: Instant data lake
he/tour.json::tour.demos.insider.summary: A bank's outbound mail matched against its watch list of deals in discussion and checked for customer data, ranked in one review queue that a first-level reviewer reads without ever seeing the list.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.insider.title: Insider review
he/tour.json::tour.demos.insurance.summa: A property insurer's question, where its exposure is concentrated against hazard risk: its own policies joined by county to FEMA, wildfire and storm data, answered in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.insurance.title: Property exposure and hazard risk
he/tour.json::tour.demos.profiling.summa: An acquired company's customers and orders, profiled by the built-in Data Profiler: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, landed as governed tables and read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.profiling.title: What is actually in this data?
he/tour.json::tour.demos.quality.summary: A chain of shops' sales feed refined from bronze to silver and gold by checked materialized views: landing a batch is all it takes, and a batch that fails a check never reaches silver.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.quality.title: Data you can trust
he/tour.json::tour.demos.reviews.summary: An electronics shop's catalog, reviews and purchases in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and Neo4j, joined on the product: which products do reviews say the battery dies on, and what else did their buyers buy?
he/tour.json::tour.demos.reviews.title: Product reviews
he/tour.json::tour.demos.sonnets.summary: The 154 sonnets embedded, searched by meaning and grown into a graph: the themes they share and the lines where Shakespeare echoes himself.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.sonnets.title: Shakespeare's sonnets
he/tour.json::tour.demos.streaming.summa: A coffee shop's orders arrive live on Kafka and are joined to its catalog: a view of the busiest regions in the last five minutes, refreshed by every batch that lands, answered in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached, and watched with a subscription.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.streaming.title: Live order stream
he/tour.json::tour.demos.testdata.summar: A shop's production database, read in prod as it is and in two test environments as realistic generated data, the same queries and joins answering in all three.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.testdata.title: Test data
he/tour.json::tour.demos.vulnerabilities: A software company's Dependabot alerts joined by CVE to the NVD and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities: which exploited vulnerabilities sit in our code, and how far past CISA's due date are they?
he/tour.json::tour.demos.weblogs.summary: A web shop's question, which pages are slow and which SQL makes them slow: its sources, the tables they become, the join of its two logs, and Polly's answer.
he/tour.json::tour.demos.weblogs.title: The web shop's logs

he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesAnswer.des: The stored view complaints_near_construction counts, for each neighborhood, the complaints made at an address with an active permit. Look at which neighborhood comes first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesComplaints: complaints is one table over every file named complaints_*.csv in the folder. Each month's file is part of it; a new month's file needs no table of its own.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.descr: A folder of files became a governed catalog: tables, relationships, a glossary term and a stored view, with nothing loaded. A new month's complaints file needs no new table: the glob already names it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesDone.title: A folder became a catalog
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesFormats.de: building_permits is read from a Parquet file, as the budget is from an Excel workbook and the inspections from a JSON file. Each is a governed table like any other.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesIntro.desc: A city publishes its open data as files: 311 complaints in a CSV file a month, building permits in Parquet, the budget in Excel and inspections in JSON. drop is one files source over that folder: every file is a table, read where it lies, with no load step. The question: which neighborhoods have the most complaints near active construction?
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.descr: The relationship DRAWS joins a building permit to the complaints made at its address. The view that answers the question joins along it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesJoin.title: Complaints at permitted addresses
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesMonths.des: The complaints counted by month: each month comes from its own file, read as one table. Look for one row for each monthly file.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.descr: The same view as a REST call. Every table and view is served over REST, GraphQL and SQL alike, under the same rules.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesRest.title: The same answer over REST
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.descr: The glossary says what an open complaint is: one the city has not yet closed. Terms like this say what the catalog's data means.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.filesTerm.title: What an open complaint is
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsContro: Next, the SQL explorer runs as every role again.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAsReview: Next, the SQL explorer runs as reviewer_ben, the first-level reviewer of the trading, research and operations desks.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderAudit.de: ops.queries records every statement: who ran it, as which role, over which table. The reviewer's reads of the queue and the watch list are here, as are yours.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderCustomer: The same mail is checked for customer data by SQL patterns: social security and account numbers. The customer table's columns are tagged pii, so this read is itself recorded.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.des: Watch-list deals were matched against outbound mail by name and by meaning, ranked for review, and the list itself was never shown to the reviewer. This is post-review analytics behind real-time controls, not a replacement for data-loss prevention. Attachments, images, encoded text and personal channels are outside it. Monitoring employees needs disclosure and, in places, a works-council agreement.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderDone.tit: What this is, and is not
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderIntro.de: Northgate Partners, an invented bank, keeps a watch list of the deals it is working on. The question: is anyone sending deal-sensitive or customer data out of the bank? bank is its database: the watch list, the employees and their mail, and the customers and who read their records. Every name and record here is generated.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.des: Two of the messages behind the queue. A trader not on deal Falcon tells a personal address about it in his own words, with no name, ticker or code name, and it ranks near the top. The deal team's mail to the deal's counsel names everything, and ranks low.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderLeak.tit: A paraphrase outranks the expected mail
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMail.des: message holds the employees' outbound mail: who sent it, when, and how many recipients were outside the bank or at a personal address.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderMatch.de: deal_match is what the match_deals command found: for each message and deal, whether it names the company, an alias, the ticker or the code name, and how close it reads to the deal's description through a local embedding model. A paraphrase that avoids every name still scores.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderOverTheW: Who was brought over the wall for the deal, and so who could have known of it. The flagged sender is not among them.
Was the sender over the wall?
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderPiiAcces: ops.pii_access lists every read of a pii-tagged table: here, the read you just made. The queue does the same for the bank's staff from the bank's own access log: the operations employee who read customer records that week and then mailed customer data out ranks first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderQueue.de: One materialized view ranks every case. The match is weighted by context: a sender outside the deal's team, a recipient outside the bank or at a personal address, and a message sent before the announcement raise it; a deal-team member writing to the deal's own counterparties lowers it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderReviewer: The same queue, read as the reviewer: only the cases of the desks they review, the flagged entity shown and the deal withheld. Row rules on the mail and its matches do this; nothing is copied. The watch list itself is refused to them.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWatchLis: deal is the control room's watch list: each deal's company, the names it goes by, its ticker, its project code name and whether it is public yet. It is the most restricted table here: the control room reads it, a deal team only its own deal, and a first-level reviewer never.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insiderWhyFlagg: Polly helps the human reviewer after the fact. Its answer was made when the demo was built, and is shown as stored.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceAnswer: The view exposure_by_county joins the book to the risk in each county, and is kept stored. Ordered by insured value weighted by risk percentile, it puts the counties where the most exposure meets the highest risk first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceBook.d: Each policy in force, read live from the insurer's own database: its county, line of business, total insured value, premium and deductible.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceByRati: The same view grouped by FEMA's risk rating: how much of the book's insured value sits in counties rated Relatively High or Very High.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceGovdat: The government data comes from AskAmerica, a live account. Its three county tables are landed once, when the demo is built, and read from that copy for good: they never expire, and this demo never calls the account.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceJoin.d: The book and the public risk tables share the county's FIPS code, and these relationships join them. Every query that crosses them uses this join.
The insurer's own data, read live, and public risk data, landed once, joined by county in one governed model: one view answers where the exposure meets the risk, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, under each role's access.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and summed on the server. Any client that speaks HTTP gets the answer without writing SQL.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceRisk.d: Every US county's all-hazard risk score and rating, its national percentile, its expected annual loss and the value of all its buildings. The wildfire and storm tables sit beside it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.insuranceScenar: A property insurer wants to know where its exposure is concentrated against natural-hazard risk. Its own book of policies, with the total insured value of each, is in its database; the hazard risk of every US county is public, in FEMA's, the US Forest Service's and NOAA's data. The tour shows Provisa joining the two, by county, and answering the question in SQL, over REST and in GraphQL.
The glossary names what an underwriter asks about: total insured value, accumulation, probable maximum loss, expected annual loss. Here accumulation: exposure concentrated where one event reaches many policies.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingAnswer: The view customer_columns keeps each customers column as the latest run found it, emptiest first. A fifth of the customers never answered the marketing question; some emails are missing and some hold a name instead; signup dates start at a 1900-01-01 placeholder, and lifetime values run from refunds below zero to test accounts at 999,999.99.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingCountr: The five commonest values of the country column: US, USA and United States are one country, written three ways among them alone. A count by country would split it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingDuplic: The model declares customer_id the key, but the export held no constraint: 150 customers are in it twice, every field the same. The profile counts the repeated rows and the key values held by more than one row.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingMember: The customers and orders tables are members of the profiler. From a member's editor you can run a profile at once or view its runs: each run, its rows and how long it took.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingPhones: Each phone number reduced to its shape: a digit becomes 9. The CRM never checked the format, so one column holds four of them, which a join or a dialer would have to reconcile first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingProfil: A profiler holds a schedule and its run settings, nothing else: this one runs every night at 02:00. Its first run was made when the demo was built, so the results are already here.
The acquired tables, read live, and a profile of them made by the built-in profiler and kept as governed tables: nulls, ranges, formats, plausible types and duplicates, each answering what is actually in this data, in SQL, GraphQL and REST, under each role's access.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRest.d: The view is a REST endpoint too. A data quality tool or a migration script gets the profile without writing SQL.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingRuns.d: A run's results land as tables of their own, one for each kind of measure, and every run is kept beside the ones before it. Here are the customers table's runs, with the rows each read and the repeated rows it found.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.profilingScenar: An outdoor retailer has bought a smaller one, Harbor Outfitters, and received its CRM's customers and orders. Before anyone builds on them, the question is: what is actually in this data? Provisa's built-in Data Profiler answers it, and its results are governed tables like any other, read in SQL, GraphQL and REST.
Data profile, plausible type, value shape, duplicate row and placeholder value, in the glossary, each tied to the measures it is about.
The profile infers what a column holds from its values, its name and its tags: an email, a phone number, a postal code, an identifier. Each comes with its confidence and the evidence for it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityAdmitted: Every silver row carries the run id of the checks that admitted its batch. The relationship ADMITTED_BY joins it to those checks in dq_results.
From a row to the checks that admitted it
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.d: bronze holds every batch as it landed, never changed. Clean data is typed on landing: the sale id, when it was sold, the quantity. The messy fields, shop code, product and price, stay raw until silver. Its probe watches it, so a new batch refreshes every view after it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityBronze.t: Bronze: typed where it is clean
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityChecks.d: dq_results is a materialized view that computes the checks in SQL on every landed batch: how many rows fail each, and pass or fail. Batch 1 passes them all; batch 2 fails three.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityDone.des: Landing a batch refreshed the checks, silver and gold, with nothing else run. The clean batch reached gold; the bad one stopped at bronze, and why is a query.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityGold.des: Gold is one GROUP BY over silver: sales, items, revenue and the price range by day and product, from checked data only.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityIntro.de: A chain of five shops sends its sales as a feed, a batch a day, landed as bronze into sales, the chain's database. Everything after bronze is a materialized view: the checks, silver and gold, refreshed by landing alone. The question: can I trust this data before it reaches gold?
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.desc: The products of the first batch as they landed: one product in several spellings, such as COFFEE, Coffee and cofee. Silver makes them one.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityRaw.titl: Raw, as the feed spelled it
The rows of batch 2 that fail a check, still in bronze as they landed: a shop the chain does not have, negative quantities, prices that are not numbers. None of batch 2 reaches silver; batch 1 stays.
What the bad batch failed on
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualitySilver.d: Silver is bronze cleaned, from the passing batches only: shop codes trimmed and upper-cased, one spelling a product, the price a number, the day derived, and a sale sent twice kept once, at its latest.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.qualityWhichChe: A silver sale and, along ADMITTED_BY, every check of the run that admitted it: each one passed, with no failing rows.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBatteryD: The shop's first question, in SQL: the reviews that say "battery dies", counted by product, with each product's ratings. One statement reads an Elasticsearch search and two MongoDB tables, and a handful of products stand out.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsBoughtWi: The second question, in Cypher: the products rated under three stars, and what their buyers also bought. The graph runs across the MongoDB ratings and the Neo4j purchases, and power banks keep turning up.
An electronics shop wants to know which products disappoint, and what their buyers do about it. The answer is spread over three NoSQL stores. This one, catalog, is MongoDB: a document for each product, its specs nested, and the star ratings customers give.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsCypherTa: bought_together is a Cypher query against Neo4j, registered as a table: for each product, every other product its buyers bought, and how many of them did.
A Cypher query as a table
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsDone.des: Three NoSQL stores, a MongoDB pipeline, an Elasticsearch search and a Cypher query, joined on the product and asked the shop's question in SQL, Cypher, REST and GraphQL.
An example query: the battery complaints in GraphQL, each review's highlighted text with its product nested beneath it through the relationship.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsGraphSto: purchases is Neo4j: 2,000 customers, each linked by a BOUGHT relationship to the products they bought. All three stores name a product by the same id.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsJoin.des: Relationships join the tables on the product id across all three stores. COMPLAINS_ABOUT joins a matching review to its product in the catalog, so a query reaches from Elasticsearch to MongoDB without spelling out the join.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsPipeline: ratings_by_product is a MongoDB aggregation pipeline, registered as a table: it groups the star ratings by product and gives each product's count, average and one-star ratings. A query reads it like any other table.
A MongoDB pipeline as a table
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsRest.des: The same search as a REST call, its phrase passed as a parameter. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed tables, so REST answers as SQL and GraphQL do, under the same rights.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchSt: reviews is Elasticsearch: the 5,000 reviews customers wrote, each with its product, its stars and its text. Provisa reads it live; nothing is copied first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.reviewsSearchTa: reviews_matching is an Elasticsearch search, registered as a table. Its phrase is a parameter: a query sets it, and each row is a review whose text holds the phrase, with the phrase highlighted.
An Elasticsearch search as a table
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsDone.des: Shakespeare's lines went from Postgres rows to Qdrant vectors, governed searches and a graph of echoes and themes.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoNetw: The echo network, drawn by Cypher: the lines that closely echo a line of another sonnet, and the sonnets they are in. Look for the sonnets joined by more than one echo.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsEchoes.d: The echo table. The command link_echoes asks the vector store for each line's three nearest lines in other sonnets and writes them here, each with its similarity.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsGraph.de: Three relationships make the tables a graph: a line is IN its sonnet, EVOKES a theme and ECHOES a line of another sonnet, with its score. Cypher walks them like any graph.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsIntro.de: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets in Postgres, embedded into Qdrant, searched by meaning, grown into a graph. The question: which themes run through the sonnets, and where does Shakespeare echo himself? sonnets is the Postgres source, a row for each sonnet and for each of its 2,155 lines.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsLines.de: The line table holds a row for each of the 2,155 lines. The command embed_lines is one governed SQL statement: its embed() turns each line's words into a vector, and the rows are written to Qdrant through the collection's write route.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsSearch.d: lines_like is a search table: Provisa reads it live in Qdrant under the arguments the statement gives it, here a phrase and how many lines to find. Look at each line's score: how near it is to the phrase.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemeVie: Each theme view stores one fixed search, joined back to the lines it found, with each line's score. This one holds the twenty lines nearest to "the ravages of time"; four more hold beauty, mortality, jealousy and verse that outlives death.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.sonnetsThemesBy: For each theme, how many of the lines it found are in the Fair Youth sonnets and how many in the Dark Lady sonnets. Look for a theme that belongs to one sequence.
vectors is Qdrant. It holds a point for each line, its vector the embedding of the line's words, and Provisa reads and writes it as it does any other source.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step0.descripti:
🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. Leave whenever — click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is one model that holds your data, its metadata and the processing between them. The same model defines your data estate and operates it — it is all one thing, and it stays out of the data path.

That is why everything stays in sync, and why reuse is built in: a relationship, metric, mask or rule defined once serves every surface, environment and role. Duplicate tables and metrics, duplicate commands and rules, even two systems serving the same data sit side by side in the model, so duplication is easy to see and simple to remove.

It is compact, extensible and composable. It slots in beside what you have, brings order to the sprawl, and lets every data professional apply their expertise without limiting their imagination — it only removes the drudgery.

🎯 The core is one short exercise: connect a database, then query it in the language or tool you already use — or just ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop, with no infrastructure to stand up.

he/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.descript:
A relationship does two jobs. It shapes your data model: how tables across sources and domains connect — which is what every query surface follows, whether GraphQL nesting, Cypher paths or SQL joins.

It is also a rule. Joins are governed: a role without the ignore_relationships right can join only along registered relationships, so which ones exist decides which queries are legal. Grant that right deliberately to a role you trust and it joins freely (never in high-security mode).

Relationships link tables across sources — even across different databases — turning flat tables into a traversable graph.

🛡️ Because a relationship is a rule, adding, changing or removing one can make a query legal or illegal. A relationship requested from outside the source table's domain, or by someone who may not create relationships, waits for approval.

he/tour.json::tour.steps.step2.descripti: ➕ New connections start with this button — PostgreSQL, Snowflake, MongoDB, a REST API, a CSV, and 50+ more.

he/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descript:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here — no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views — over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands — governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data — invokable from every surface, fully governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts — declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics — governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once; every surface — SQL, GraphQL, AI agents — computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descript:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars — recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar, not just a clock.
  • 🗄️ Store As… — replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel — bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descript:
🧬 Lineage is the dependency trail your derivations leave: what each view, calculated column or metric is built from, and what depends on it. This is a real query, analyzed — follow name_upper back through its transforms to the exact source columns that feed it.

Nothing runs — the query is only analyzed.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
he/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descript:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine — pluggable: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime — the model, the surfaces, and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach — Parquet, Iceberg, Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials auto-provisioned. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability — redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management
  • 📤 Export the model's configuration — the whole model or chosen sections — as a file to review, diff and ship through CI/CD

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step — no rewrite:

  • Develop — embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale — Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote — point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.

SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source — join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. And the model's own metadata and every activity trace are themselves queryable tables here — join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 Not just this explorer — the same governed SQL runs through multiple wire protocols; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire — every Postgres-compatible client — psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI — connects out of the box.
  • JDBC — drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline, or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL — columnar streaming for ADBC clients — no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport — ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.

he/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 7 surfaces)
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.descr: 🗄️ These layers are separate. The response cache holds query results, and a request opts in with @cached or a SQL comment. Small lookup tables are mirrored to speed joins. A replica of a source table that cannot be attached lives in the durable store, beside materialized views.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.title: Caches and replicas
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCommands.de: ⚡ A command is a governed, typed operation, such as an HTTP service, a Python model or a stored procedure. Register it once and call it from every surface, with the same rights and tracing as a query.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDataProduct:
📦 Every product here speaks ODPS (the Open Data Product Standard) — owner, team, purpose, limitations, usage, SLA, support, custom properties — and Provisa auto-publishes it straight into Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex, so it shows up as a native product in the catalog your consumers already use.

🔁 There's no separate export step to forget: the spec is derived from the live model — tables, lineage, tags, glossary terms — every time, so what's published can't drift out of date the way a hand-maintained ODPS file would.

✅ Publishing also sends an ontology extract: the part of your glossary that bears on what is published — the terms that define its columns, the broader and related terms they connect to, and the typed relationships between them. The data-quality results of the checkers that scan it go with it. A product's Related Terms panel lists its terms.
Data products, published where consumers already look
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDomains.des: 🗂️ A domain groups tables, and its data steward governs that part of the model: who sees what, masks and row rules, sensitive data, and its glossary and data products.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepEnvKinds.de: An environment is a branch of your model, and the list shows which one each was made from. When you create one, Inherit connections reads that environment's source connections by reference, so a rotation there is picked up here. Leave it off, the default, to get the whole model with none of the connections, and point each source at your own database.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.descr: 🎭 The Testing tab of a table's Columns shows each column's fake, such as email(). Fake only the identifying columns and keep the rest real. A column can also carry a synthetic rule, used only when generating synthetic data.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.title: Declare a fake
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakesFill.d: ✨ Fill from profile proposes fakes for identifying columns, and synthetic rules for the rest, from the table's latest profile. Nothing saves until you save the form.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary.de: 📖 Every term links to the columns that carry it and to other terms — curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps: ✨ Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and ✨ Relationships proposes links across the whole glossary. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossaryTer: 📖 A term names one business concept, lists the columns that carry it, links to the terms it relates to and says what it means. Terms for real columns are derived for you; add one by hand for a concept no single column carries.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepMetrics.des: 📏 A metric is the business definition of a measure, an aggregate over one fact table. Define it once and SQL, GraphQL, the explore canvas and every view built from it compute the same number; a view regenerates when its metric changes.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepObservabili: 🔭 Tracing records one span per request. The Debug tracing tab adds a span per pipeline stage and per source call, with SQL text. It adds load, so turn it on for one org, role or source for a set time; it turns itself off when the time is up.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.descr:
💬 Polly sets Provisa up in plain language — much easier than reading the docs.

“register my Postgres” · “fake the email column in the customers table” · “create a QA environment on synthetic data” · “who can see salaries?”

Polly works through the same governed APIs and rights as the UI, so it can only do what you can. Polly is open here; the chat button reopens this panel anytime.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.title: Meet Polly, your setup assistant
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPreview.des: 👀 Expand a row and click Preview — live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProductForm: 📦 Name the owner and team, the purpose, usage, SLA and support, then pick the tables and commands it contains. These are the fields that get published. A table joins a product only when both share the same domain.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProfilerChe: Every run adds rows to its result tables: columns (null share, distinct count, range), runs (row count), children per parent, quantiles and drift. Register a result table and a data-quality checker, a Soda or Great Expectations source like any other, can scan it, so any measure a profile produces can carry a check that raises an issue. Drift is one such measure: each run is compared with the table's recent runs, and a measure that moves is flagged. An accepted constraint, a drift check, or a check against expectations from outside Provisa can be added to the checker's contract from the profiler's runs.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.des:
📤 Publish it where your org already looks. Catalog entries (tables, columns, domains, stewards, approved relationships), data products and column-level lineage go out, and each target receives what it supports: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Collibra, Atlan and Apache Atlas as catalogs, Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex as data-product listings, and lineage over OpenLineage.

Publication is outbound only: Provisa never reads a target back as a source of truth.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPublish.tit: Publish to the tools your org uses
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityPane: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column — null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness — and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProd: ✅ A product's Data Quality panel lists the checker tables whose contracts scan its output ports, so a consumer sees the evidence next to the product. It is empty until a checker scans one. Data products are published in the Publish it Deep Dive.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityProf: 📊 A table joins a Data Profiler on its editor's Quality tab, a source that profiles its member tables on a schedule. A run measures each column's shape, distributions and value frequencies, and the children per parent. Run Profile Now starts one and View Profile Runs reads them. Results land as tables you register and govern like any other; until you register them, no reader sees a profile. The next card puts checks on them.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityTabl: 🧪 A data-quality checker — Soda or Great Expectations — registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.
A quality checker is just a source
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.descr: 💬 You ask in the language or tool you already use — SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, plain language through Polly, or a BI tool or driver — and every one reads the same governed model, so the answer and the rules are the same whichever you pick.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.title: Query it your way
🤖 The model and its relationships are available to AI agents — Polly, and agents connecting over MCP — and they shape the queries those agents write.

An agent runs under a role, so the same rule applies to it as to a person: a query that joins outside the registered relationships fails. This is enforced, not advisory.

It is also your choice. To let an agent discover relationships, grant its role the ignore_relationships right; to keep it inside guardrails, leave the role without it. It is the same deliberate grant as for a trusted identity (never honored in high-security mode).
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsList.de: 📋 The model's relationships, whether or not a source declares them, filterable and sortable. Expand a row to edit it or add its reverse. A role joins only along these relationships unless it holds the ignore_relationships right.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsSuggest: ✨ The sparkle button looks for likely joins: it reads the foreign keys your sources declare and, when an AI model key is configured, asks the model to infer more. Nothing is declared until you accept a candidate, and a rejected one stays out until you clear the rejections.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepReports.des: 📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports — usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health — each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRequests.de: ✋ This request comes from someone who may not create relationships themselves, often from outside your domain, wanting to relate their tables to yours — usually the first step toward asking for your data. Relationships are governed, so approving one changes which queries are legal: a role that may join only along approved relationships can now join across it. A relationship request needs two approvals before it can be executed. A relationship across two domains needs a yes from each side. Approve it, execute it, or reject it with a reason from a fixed list; resolved requests move to the Resolved tab.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRoleInherit: 👪 A role can inherit from a parent: it receives the parent's grants, column visibility and row rules, and its own row rule for a table replaces the parent's. The role also carries its capabilities and its rate and complexity limits.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepScheduled.d: ⏱️ Run a webhook, a SQL statement or a command on a cron schedule, when a table changes, or on a table's error or quarantine. A trigger runs as a role you choose, so governance applies, and each shows how its last run ended.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSynthetic.d: 🧪 In the Synthetic data tab, define a dataset from the profile runs of the tables you name and press Generate. It fills a non-production environment with rows shaped like those tables, with the same relationships and fan-out, at the scale you choose. A comparison report shows how close it came.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSyntheticPr: 🔒 Declare a dataset private with a privacy budget ε. Calibrated noise is added to every statistic the generator draws from a profile, and the report states what the noise dropped.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.descri: 🏷️ A tag is one org-wide label with a fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships or commands. Tags carry behavior, not only documentation, and a tag can require a reason, an expiry date or a parameter when it is applied.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.title: Tags carry meaning
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataMap:
Safe, realistic data to build and test against comes from four parts, each with one job:

  • Environment: a branch of the model. At creation it inherits its parent's connections or starts unbound, and you point its sources at your own databases.
  • Profiler: measures real tables, giving the shapes everything else is built from.
  • Fakes: in test data, a column's fake replaces its identifying values.
  • Synthetic data: fills a non-production environment with generated rows shaped like the profiled tables.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTestDataPro: 📊 A Data Profiler measures the tables you add to it: column shapes, distributions, value frequencies and children per parent. Fill from profile turns those measures into fakes, and a synthetic dataset draws its rows from them. Watching the same runs for drift is covered in the Data quality Deep Dive.
What fakes and synthetic data are built from
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingAnswer: orders_last_five_minutes is a materialized view: each region's orders and revenue in the last five minutes. Every batch of orders that lands refreshes it, so this read is of stored rows a few seconds old, never of the topic. Run it again in a minute and the numbers have moved.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCached: The same view in GraphQL. @cached(ttl: 10) asks for the response cache: the same question within ten seconds is answered from the cache, and the X-Provisa-Cache header says HIT.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingCatalo: catalog is the shop's Postgres, read live: what each product is and costs, and the regions the shop sells in.
The latest orders in the table, a few seconds behind the topic. Each sandbox lands the whole topic into its own table, under its own consumer group.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingJoin.d: PLACED_IN joins each order to its region, and ORDERED to its product, so an order's revenue comes from the catalog's price.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingLive.d: A GraphQL subscription on the orders: every batch that lands sends the latest orders again, as it lands. Leave it running and watch the list move.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingOrders: orders is the topic, landed into a table of its own as the orders arrive: a batch at most every two seconds, each order by its id. Every batch that lands refreshes the views that read it, and tells its subscribers.
A Kafka topic landed as a table and joined to a live catalog; a view kept current by every batch that lands; the same answer in SQL, GraphQL and REST, cached on request; and a subscription that moves with the feed. Look around on your own from the query page.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingRest.d: The same view as a REST call, for a dashboard that polls it.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.streamingScenar: A coffee shop's orders arrive on a Kafka topic, a few a second, and its catalog is in its Postgres. The question: which regions placed the most orders in the last five minutes? orders is the broker the orders arrive on.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDev.des: The same statement, read in dev: every column is its fake, computed by the engine as it reads. Names, emails, cities and dates look real and are not. Nothing was copied out of production.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevAnsw: A view joining orders, their lines, customers and products answers in dev too. Grouping, joining and adding up all run on the fakes, so a test exercises the same queries production runs.
Views and joins work on the fakes
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDevGrap: Each order with the customer who placed it, through the relationship. Every API reads the environment it is served from, so a test suite against GraphQL, REST or SQL sees the same generated data.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataDone.de: Environments are branches of one model, and a fake is declared once per column. A Test (fake) environment answers every query with realistic generated values, keeps keys joinable, and is refused while a personal-data column has no fake. Production data never leaves production.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataJoin.de: An order's customer_id and the customer's id are both faked as a hash. One real value always gives the same fake, so an order still finds its customer when both are fake.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProd.de: In prod, the environment a request naming none is served, the customers read as they are.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataProdAns: The same view, read in prod: the real revenue by region and category. Only prod is served real rows; dev and test never see them.
The real answer, in production only
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataScenari: shop-db is a shop's production database: its customers, products and orders. Developers and testers need data of the same shape to work against, but the customers' names, emails and cities are personal data, and copies of production drift. The data here is itself generated, to stand in for a real shop.
Can I test against realistic data without touching production?
Every column of customers names the kind of value it holds, its fake: a person's name, an email address, a city, one of four regions, a date in a range. The model carries it with the column, so the fake is defined once, where the column is.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataTest.de: A real value shows the same fake wherever it is read, so dev and test agree: a test written in dev finds the same rows in test.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.testdataToDev.d: dev and test are environments of the model: branches of it, as in git. Both are Test (fake) environments. Next, the header's switcher moves to dev; every read after it is served from there.
Next, the switcher returns to prod.
Next, the switcher moves to test, the second Test (fake) environment.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.vulnerabilities: One alert for each pinned package version with a published advisory: the repository, the package, the CVE, the version that fixes it, and whether the alert is open, fixed or dismissed. It is read live from the company's database.
The Dependabot alerts

The view exploited_in_our_code keeps each open alert whose CVE is in CISA's catalog, with the days since CISA's due date passed, and is kept stored. Internet-facing repositories first, longest overdue first: where to start.
The answer in SQL
The same view, grouped by team on the server: how many exploited vulnerabilities each team has open, and how long the oldest has been overdue.
The answer in GraphQL

The government data comes from AskAmerica, a live account: the NVD's CVE records, MITRE's catalog of software weaknesses and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities. Its tables are landed once, when the demo is built, and read from that copy for good: this demo never calls the account.
The public vulnerability data
The same joins as a graph in Cypher: repositories, the open alerts raised in them, their CVEs and the catalog entries that mark them exploited.
The answer as a graph
A CVE record and its entry in CISA's catalog share the CVE identifier, and this relationship joins them. With the alerts joined to their CVEs, an alert reaches the catalog in two steps.
Exploited, by CVE
Each CVE that attackers are known to exploit, with the date federal agencies must fix it by and whether ransomware campaigns use it. Landed whole: it is small.
CISA's known exploited vulnerabilities

The NVD holds a quarter of a million CVEs, and the company's alerts name nineteen. The table's landing filter, a condition on its own columns, keeps only those when the table is landed, so the copy holds just the records the alerts need.
The CVE records, landed through a filter

The company's own code data, read live, and public vulnerability data, landed once and only as much of it as the alerts need, joined by CVE in one governed model: one view answers which exploited vulnerabilities sit in the code and how overdue each is, in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.
What you saw
The view is a REST endpoint too, grouped and counted on the server. A ticketing system or a dashboard gets the answer without writing SQL.
The same answer over REST

A software company wants to know which of the vulnerabilities in its code attackers actually exploit, and how long each has gone unfixed. Its repositories, their packages and the Dependabot alerts on them are in its own database; the CVE records and CISA's catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities are public. The tour shows Provisa joining the two by CVE and answering the question in SQL, GraphQL, Cypher and REST.
What this demo is

Known exploited vulnerability, CVE, CWE and CVSS, in the company's glossary, each tied to the columns it is about. A CVSS score says how severe a vulnerability is; only the catalog says whether anyone exploits it.
The vocabulary
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsDone.des: Three sources became tables, joined on a request id, and answered the shop's question in SQL and over REST.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsJoin.des: nginx gives every request an id, and the shop names each database connection after it. The LOGGED_FOR relationship tells Provisa to join a statement to its request on that id, so no query has to spell out the join.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsLogFiles: The shop has three sources: shop-db, its PostgreSQL database, and two log sources, shop_access and shop_db_log. Provisa reads each log file where it sits, one line to a row, and again every 30 seconds; nothing is loaded or copied first.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsRest.des: The slowest pages again, as a REST call: each path with its request count and its average and longest time. Every surface Provisa serves reads the same governed model, so REST gives the answer SQL or GraphQL would, under the same rights.
A small web shop wants to know which pages are slow, and which SQL makes them slow. The answer is split across nginx's access log, the database's statement log and the shop's own database. The tour shows how Provisa reads log files as tables, joins them across sources and governs them by role, then answers the question in SQL and over REST.
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsStatemen: The slowest pages joined to the statements their requests ran, in plain SQL over two of the demo's views. A view is a saved query that Provisa expands into this statement before it runs. Here is where the time went, statement by statement.
The SQL behind a slow page
he/tour.json::tour.steps.weblogsTables.d: Each source's data is registered as tables: the shop's customers, products and orders, and one table for each log, its lines split into columns such as path, status and time. Views, saved queries over them, add the slowest pages and the SQL each request ran.
